question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=7 x^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)=\left(3 x + 5\right)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=14 x,\quad v'(x)=18 x + 30.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(14 x)(\left(3 x + 5\right)^{2})-(7 x^{2})(18 x + 30)}{(\left(3 x + 5\right)^{2})^2} \\ & =\frac{70 x}{\left(3 x + 5\right)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: All real x where the displayed denominator is nonzero.

We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\left(x + 3\right)^{2}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x^{2} + 9.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=2 x + 6,\quad v'(x)=2 x.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(2 x + 6)(x^{2} + 9)-(\left(x + 3\right)^{2})(2 x)}{(x^{2} + 9)^2} \\ & =- \frac{6 \left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)}{\left(x^{2} + 9\right)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\cos{\left(3 x \right)}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=- 3 \sin{\left(3 x \right)},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(- 3 \sin{\left(3 x \right)})(x)-(\cos{\left(3 x \right)})(1)}{(x)^2} \\ & =- \frac{3 x \sin{\left(3 x \right)} + \cos{\left(3 x \right)}}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value at $x=\frac{3 \pi}{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y'(\frac{3 \pi}{2}) & =- \frac{2}{\pi} \\ & =- \frac{2}{\pi}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: All real x where the displayed denominator is nonzero.

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=e^{4 x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=4 e^{4 x},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(4 e^{4 x})(x)-(e^{4 x})(1)}{(x)^2} \\ & =\frac{\left(4 x - 1\right) e^{4 x}}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value at $x=6$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y'(6) & =\frac{23 e^{24}}{36} \\ & =\frac{23 e^{24}}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(t)=2 t$ and the denominator $v(t)=\left(4 t^{2} + 6\right)^{2}.$ 

Differentiating $u(t)$ and $v(t),$ we have

$$
u'(t)=2,\quad v'(t)=16 t \left(4 t^{2} + 6\right).
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\prime}(t) & =\frac{u'(t)v(t)-u(t)v'(t)}{[v(t)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(2)(\left(4 t^{2} + 6\right)^{2})-(2 t)(16 t \left(4 t^{2} + 6\right))}{(\left(4 t^{2} + 6\right)^{2})^2} \\ & =- \frac{3 \left(2 t^{2} - 1\right)}{2 \left(2 t^{2} + 3\right)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: t > 0; a,b,c are positive.

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ and the denominator $v(x)=x.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x),\,{v}^{′}(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))(x)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))(1)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{-3(\frac{\pi }{2})sin\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})-cos\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})}{{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-3(\frac{\pi }{2})(-1)-0}{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: All real x where the displayed denominator is nonzero.

question.:question/worked-solution:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=e^{2 x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=x + 3.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
u'(x)=2 e^{2 x},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{u'(x)v(x)-u(x)v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\ & =\frac{(2 e^{2 x})(x + 3)-(e^{2 x})(1)}{(x + 3)^2} \\ & =\frac{\left(2 x + 5\right) e^{2 x}}{\left(x + 3\right)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value at $x=4$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}y'(4) & =\frac{13 e^{8}}{49} \\ & =\frac{13 e^{8}}{49}.\end{aligned}
$$
